title: Ang 146–150: Majh ki Var ends
tomorrow: what's heavier than anything you've ever lifted?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the majh ballad, and its bright line: what's rightfully another's is never yours. Today it ends.

A building can look holy from the street: a dome, wide steps, a sign out front. What happens inside a person is harder to photograph. So what would a mosque built out of mercy look like? As Majh ki Var heads for its last pauris, ang 146 to 150, it has already asked that question, a few pages back, and answered it with respect for its Muslim neighbors.
screen: `HOLY FROM THE STREET.` → `HARDER TO PHOTOGRAPH.` → `A MOSQUE OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: The question underneath: what makes someone truly religious? On ang 140, Guru Nanak speaks to Muslims, in paraphrase: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observance and your fast; so be a Muslim. Let good deeds be your Kaaba and truth your guide. And on ang 141: it's hard to be called a Muslim; whoever truly is one, let them be called a Muslim. He isn't mocking the mosque. He holds up the Muslim ideal and asks for it lived all the way through. Now the neighbor, in its own words. The Qur'an, surah 2, verse 177, says, in paraphrase: righteousness isn't turning your face to the east or the west. The righteous believe in God and the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture and the prophets; give wealth, out of love for Him, to relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveler; keep the prayer; keep their promises; and stay patient in hardship. The shared ground: the outward form points past itself to a life, and the life is the measure. The honest difference: in that verse, the prayer stays, alongside belief in angels, Scripture and prophets. Muslims keep it. Guru Nanak's salok turns mosque, mat and fast into virtues, and Sikhs keep their own forms: the gurdwara, the Granth, the daily prayers. Then the ballad's closing pauris finish its praise of the One, and the var is done.
screen: `WHAT MAKES SOMEONE TRULY RELIGIOUS?` · `MERCY YOUR MOSQUE, TRUTH YOUR GUIDE.` · `QUR'AN 2:177: NOT EAST OR WEST.` · `SHARED MEASURE, DIFFERENT FORMS.` · then, large: `THE BALLAD ENDS.`

segments.voice: If you can, read the last pauri on ang 150 first. Then listen for one sound near you, a voice in another room, traffic, a bird, and let it stand for a neighbor whose prayers sound different from yours. Hold that sound kindly until it fades.
Ang 146. The page where the closing pauris of Majh ki Var begin, finishing Guru Nanak's ballad.
Keep this line: the ballad ends, and its mosque of mercy stays standing. Peace to your neighbors.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape wisdom, with the weekly unity thread. Question: what makes someone truly religious? Sikh answer from Majh ki Var (ang 140–141); neighbor: Islam, in its own source (Qur'an 2:177, paraphrased from memory of the text; Pickthall not quoted to avoid any wording error). Shared: the form points to a life, and the life is the measure. Honest difference: in 2:177 the prayer and belief remain part of righteousness and Muslims keep them; the salok turns the forms into virtues and Sikhs keep their own forms. No ranking, no 'all the same'.

The teach draws mostly on ang 140–141, which the outline gives to day 1468 (ang 137–145); day 1468 used ang 137 and 141 (another's due). Today's own range, ang 146–150, is only described ('the closing pauris finish its praise of the One'). A Keeper should confirm that description, and may prefer a line from ang 146–150 itself.

Ang 140 salok paraphrase (mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an; modesty and good conduct your observance and fast; good deeds your Kaaba, truth your guide) and ang 141 (hard to be called a Muslim). Confirm Angs and wording; 'modesty your circumcision' is softened to 'observance'. A Muslim reviewer should also confirm that the framing is respectful.

Qur'an 2:177 paraphrase lists belief in God, the Last Day, angels, Scripture, prophets; giving to kin, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer; prayer; keeping promises; patience. The Prophet Muhammad is not named, so no honorific is needed. Confirm.
